body:
# Independent audit of the log-concave optimal-depth theorem

Audited file: `candidate 0f025bdf9a51573b`.


argument does not require that the chosen origin maximize the density. It
works for every real p>0. The resulting theorem is an ordinary continuous
auxiliary result, not the mixed-integer conjecture.

## Dependency graph

1. Continuity of finite concave functions on open convex sets, elementary
   integration, and convexity of superlevel sets give the density bounds.
2. Increasing one-dimensional quantile transport plus the weighted
   arithmetic-geometric mean inequality prove radial-integral convexity.
3. Absolute continuity, compactness of the sphere, a small positive-density
   ball, and Caratheodory give a deepest point with balanced active normals.
4. Polar integration and those active normals give a uniform convex body
   with exactly the same *maximum* depth.
5. The ordinary uniform-body Grunbaum inequality gives gamma_r.

The argument neither invokes a mixed-integer statement nor silently
replaces a fixed-point bound by an optimal-point bound.

## Lemma 1: bounds and support

Let U be the interior of the convex set where f is positive. Full-dimensional
support and integrability imply U is nonempty. At any selected origin in U,
log f is finite and concave on U, hence continuous, so a closed sufficiently
small ball B(0,delta) has f>=m>0.

The midpoint estimate integrates to the explicit bound

    1 >= 2^(-r) vol(B(0,delta)) sqrt(m f(x)),

valid for every x. Thus even arbitrary permitted boundary values of f
are bounded. The convex superlevel set E={f>=f(0)/2} contains a ball.
If it had points arbitrarily far away, the convex hull of such a point
and that fixed ball would contain cones with volumes tending to infinity.
This contradicts the integral bound on E. This proof does not need E to
be closed.

Choose R with E contained in the open R-ball. For s=|x|>=R and f(x)>0,
the displayed log-concavity estimate gives

    f(x) <= f(0) 2^(-s/R).

If f(x)=0 this conclusion is automatic. Enlarging a constant on the
R-ball gives the claimed global exponential majorant. No smoothness,
mode-at-origin, or compact-support assumption appears.

## Lemma 2: the critical algebra

The normalized ray measures have strictly positive continuous densities
r^(p-1)f(rx) on their open positive intervals. Their distribution functions
are C1 with positive derivative there. Thus their inverse quantiles are C1
on (0,1), including when p<1; no endpoint differentiability is asserted.

For the notation in the candidate, direct calculation gives

    a+b=1,
    a rx+b sy=t(lambda x+(1-lambda)y),
    ar+bs=t,

and

    t^(p-1)t'
      =t^p [a/(r^p f_1)+b/(s^p f_2)].

Consequently log-concavity followed by weighted AM-GM gives

    t^(p-1) f(tz)t'
      >=t^p f_1^a f_2^b
           [a/(r^p f_1)+b/(s^p f_2)]
      >=t^p/(r^(pa)s^(pb))
      >=1.

The last inequality is precisely ar+bs=t>=r^a s^b, raised to the
positive power p. All factors and exponents are correctly placed.
This calculation has no p>=1 requirement.

To formalize the change of variables, integrate first over
[eta,1-eta] for 0<eta<1/2. Since t is strictly increasing and C1 there,
the integral over [t(eta),t(1-eta)] is at least 1-2eta. Let eta decrease
to zero and use monotone convergence on the nonnegative integrand. The
quantiles tend to zero at their lower endpoints because the density is
positive immediately to the right of zero. This yields I_p(z)>=1 even
when either ray endpoint is infinite.

For continuity on the sphere, every ray from an interior point has at
most one point on the boundary of the closed support. At all other ray
parameters f is continuous in a neighborhood, or identically zero in a
neighborhood. Dominated convergence applies with the integrable bound
A t^(p-1) exp(-ct). Uniform radial upper and lower bounds then imply a
compact convex unit sublevel set with nonempty interior. Its gauge is
the continuous convex positively homogeneous function claimed.

## Lemma 3: maximum and active normals

For each halfspace containing y, moving its boundary parallel to itself
until it passes through y yields a subset with no larger measure. Hence
the depth definition equals min_u G(y,u). Because every hyperplane is
Lebesgue-null, the indicated dominated-convergence argument proves
joint continuity of G. Compact minimization on the unit sphere makes
depth continuous in y.

The outward cap through a distant y lies outside the ball of radius |y|.
Therefore depth tends to zero at infinity. The positive-density ball at
an interior point proves positive depth there. These two facts justify
attainment on a sufficiently large compact ball. A supporting halfspace
at a support-boundary point has measure zero, so every deepest point is
in the interior of the support, where Lemmas 1 and 2 apply.

For the balance argument, select the neighborhood N of active normals
with its closure inside {u:u dot v>delta/2}. For all u in N and small
epsilon, the new slab within a fixed positive-density ball around y has
thickness >=epsilon delta/2. Its sections uniformly contain a fixed
(r-1)-ball, giving a uniform increase c epsilon. This also works in r=1
using zero-dimensional section measure one. On the compact complement
of N there is a uniform positive gap above alpha. Joint continuity is
uniform on the compact set consisting of this complement times a small
closed neighborhood of y. Thus every cap stays above alpha after the
move. The contradiction proves zero belongs to the convex hull of the
active normals. Caratheodory gives at most r+1, with zero coefficients
discarded.

## Lemma 4: preservation of the maximum

With p=r, the radial function rho=r^(1/r)/q_r on the unit sphere gives
a convex body of volume one. Polar integration equates every origin
halfspace volume with the corresponding density halfspace mass. This
alone would only preserve depth at the chosen point. The additional
balanced-active-normal certificate supplies the missing optimality:
for any w, one active normal has u_i dot w>=0. The cap through w with
that normal is contained in the active origin cap and has volume <=alpha.
This proves depth_U(w)<=alpha at every w, and therefore equality of
the two global maximum values. There is no centroid-rounding step.

## Boundary and atom issues

The density is with respect to r-dimensional Lebesgue measure. It is
therefore atomless and every hyperplane has measure zero. Closed
halfspaces are used throughout; any neglect of hyperplane boundaries
in dominated convergence or polar integration discards zero measure.
The theorem assumes full-dimensional density support and r>=1. It does
not claim directly to address singular measures, lower-dimensional
mixed-integer fibers, or r=0.

## Sharpness and the simplex-gauge family

Uniform simplex measure gives the sharp constant by ordinary simplex
Grunbaum sharpness and affine vertex symmetry. For the proposed larger
family, the gauge p_T is finite convex and coercive because T is a
convex body containing zero in its interior. Thus c exp(-p_T) is an
integrable, full-dimensional, log-concave density. For any origin
halfspace H, layer cake gives

    integral_H c exp(-p_T(x)) dx
      =c integral_0^infinity e^(-t) vol(tT intersect H) dt
      =c vol(T intersect H) integral_0^infinity e^(-t)t^r dt.

After normalization its fraction is exactly vol(T intersect H)/vol(T).
Every affine vertex permutation fixes the centroid and hence becomes
a linear map fixing zero. Its determinant has absolute value one,
because it preserves T and its nonzero volume. Thus it preserves the
density measure. The average of the orbit of any point is fixed by all
vertex permutations; the only such vector is zero. Convexity of Tukey
depth superlevel sets then makes zero deepest. Its depth is gamma_r,
so the nonuniform equality example checks out.

## Minor expository changes worth making

The proof is correct without alteration. To make endpoint manipulations
fully explicit, add the [eta,1-eta] change-of-variables justification in
Lemma 2, and state explicitly in Lemma 3 why minimizing over boundaries
through y equals the original containing-halfspace depth. These are
details proved above, not theorem-strength gaps.
